title: The prayer rope
hook: a knotted wool rope, one Jesus Prayer per knot

segments.voice: Yesterday, penthos: holy grief, tears that wash rather than wound. Your line was tears that wash. Did something move you, and did you let it? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

A loop of black wool sits in a monk's hand. It isn't a string of beads. It's knots, each one tied by hand, close together, with a small woolen cross where the loop closes. His thumb finds a knot, and he says a short prayer. Then the thumb moves to the next knot. Another prayer. Then the next. Nothing about it is fancy. It would fit in a coat pocket. We've already met the Jesus Prayer in these days on the Orthodox way of the heart. Today we meet the thing in the hand that keeps it company. In Greek it's called a komboskini. In Russian it's chotki, and that's today's word.

Why knots at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians, in three words, "Pray without ceasing." For anyone who wants to take that at its word, a rope helps: a way to keep going without losing your place, or your attention. It's cheap, quiet and always to hand. There's a story told about the knots. Tradition says a monk tied knots in a cord to keep count of his prayers, and the devil kept coming in the night and untying them. So he was shown a new kind of knot, woven out of little crosses, that the devil couldn't undo. It's a legend, but it says plainly what the rope is for: a prayer, tied tight. The prayer itself is short. Its usual form asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner. Its words echo the Gospels. A blind man by the road at Jericho shouts, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." A tax collector in the temple won't even lift his eyes, and prays, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two together and you can hear it. Now notice what the rope is not. It isn't a scoreboard. In this tradition the point is attention, not the total. The knot under the thumb is there to bring a wandering mind back, gently, the way a friend's hand on your shoulder does. Lose your place, and you simply carry on from the next knot, the wool still warm from your thumb.

Here's the practice: tie knots in a string and pray. Take a shoelace, a thread, a phone charger if that's all you've got. Tie a few knots in it, slowly. Then hold it, and let your thumb find the first knot. If you pray, you can say the Jesus Prayer, once for each knot. If you don't, breathe in and out once for each knot, and let each one be a single moment of attention. When your mind wanders, the next knot calls you back. The bell holds the time.
Chotki. The Orthodox prayer rope: knotted wool, one Jesus Prayer for each knot, and a thumb that keeps the place.
Your line: a knot, a prayer. Keep your knotted string in your pocket today. Each time your hand finds it, give it one knot: one prayer, or one breath. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Orthodox monks and lay people pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted wool rope, moving the thumb one knot for each prayer; in Greek it is called a komboskini, in Russian chotki.

fork.setup: you're halfway around the prayer rope and realize your mind wandered and you've lost count. what do you do?
options: start the whole rope over, and get it perfect this time.

fork.reveal: the rope can help keep count, but the point is attention, not a perfect total. you pick up at the next knot and carry on.

notes: The Jesus Prayer is described, not quoted ('asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner'); confirm that rendering of the usual form is acceptable.
Knot legend given as 'tradition says' and 'a legend'; in some tellings an angel shows St Pachomius the knot. Left unnamed. Confirm.

Description of the rope (black wool, knots woven from small crosses, a woolen cross where the loop closes) is general; ropes vary in color and some have beads or tassels. No knot counts given on purpose.
Original: чётки (CHOT-kee, more exactly CHYOT-kee) and κομποσκοίνι (also spelled κομβοσκοίνι). Check spelling and transliteration 'komboskini'.
'In three words' counts 'Pray without ceasing' (KJV). 'Jericho' for Mark 10:46–47 is in the text.
'Nobody is counting but God, and God isn't keeping that kind of count' is a light line; check it doesn't read as speaking for God.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced history of why monks needed a rope; 'its roots are in the Gospels' softened to 'its words echo the Gospels'; cut the closing line that spoke for God ('God isn't keeping that kind of count') and ended on a concrete detail instead.

Audit: hook's garbled 'In Russian, and today's word: chotki' rewritten; fork reveal no longer says the rope is 'not to keep a tally', since the teach's own legend has a monk tying knots to keep count (ropes are also used to keep a rule of prayer).
